system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 20 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2172-07-16 15:05:00 to 2172-08-05 15:05:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted electively for high-dose cyclophosphamide chemotherapy as part of stem cell mobilization for multiple myeloma treatment. He tolerated the chemotherapy well without acute adverse events, nausea, or complications. His insulin regimen was adjusted downward following discontinuation of dexamethasone, with guidance from the endocrine service. Coumadin was held due to anticipated thrombocytopenia from chemotherapy. Lamivudine was initiated for hepatitis B reactivation prophylaxis given a positive core antibody. He was discharged home the following day with instructions to start Neupogen and ciprofloxacin, continue adjusted diabetes medications, and hold anticoagulation until further guidance from his oncologist.
problems: Multiple myeloma, without mention of having achieved remission
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Other and unspecified alcohol dependence, unspecified

velcade/revlamid/dexamethasone.  Initially, transplant was 
delayed due to transaminitis.  Biopsy of the liver was performed 
prior to admission without cirrhosis.  The patient tolerated the 
transplant well.  Prior to discharge, he was eating and drinking 
well, and was ambulating without issue. Bactrim and acyclovir 
were used for prophylaxis. Neupogen was used post transplant 
until counts recovered.  He had a non-tunneled central line 
placed by ___ after line placement on the floor was not 
successful.  This line was pulled without incident prior to 
discharge
.
#) Diverticulitis:  On D+3 the patient developed abdominal pain, 
and CT was consistent with acute diverticulitis.  He was 
initially covered with meropenem, which was transistioned to PO 
cipro/flagyl after count recovery, with plan for 2 week total 
course from date of initial count recovery.  He was pain free 
for several days prior to discharge
.
# Loose Tooth:  While counts were low, the patient developed 
what he described as a ""loose tooth."" Exam was not consistent 
with infection, and his symptoms resolved after 2 days.  
Encouraged patient to follow-up with a dentist for full 
examination in the future.
.
#) Edema: In the setting of high IVF the patient developed some 
lower extremity edema (occasionally took lasix at home prior to 
admission).  IV lasix was used with improvement
.
#) IDDM:  ___ was consulted and upon discharge recommended a 
sliding scale, 25u of glargine, and to follow-up with his 
outpatient endocrinologist within ___ hours of discharge. The 
patient was counseled on this, and to carefully monitor and 
record his sugars.  He demonstrated a good understanding
.
#) HTN: Increased amlodipine to 10mg daily, and continued home 
atenolol.
.
#) HBV core ab +: Surveillance ___ HBV viral load NEGATIVE.  
Started lamivudine ___
.
#) Tuberculosis exposure (h/o +PPD):  Evaluated by Infectious 
Disease shortly before admission.  Per their recommendations:
-300 mg isoniazid with pyridoxine 50 mg by mouth daily once his 
counts have recovered following the stem cell infusion.
-Start on prophylaxis about ___ days after count recovery.  
-___ need to consider extension of the standard nine-month 
therapy of INH if the patient continues to have frequent trips 
to ___ which would put him at risk for reinfection. 
-Need to monitor side effects of the INH including 
hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy, which are both current 
problems for him for other reasons.  
-LFTs every two weeks at the beginning of treatment given h/o 
transaminitis.
.
#) Transaminititis:  Chronic issue.  Attributed in part to 
alcohol use.  His LFTs began increasing prior to discharge, and 
he was instructed to follow-up closely with his outpatient 
doctors
.
#) Neuropathy: Continued nortryptiline; Gabapentin was stopped
#) supplementation: vitamin d.
#) FULL CODE CONFIRMED
.
==============
TRANSITIONAL ISSUES:
-Needs very close monitoring of his LFTS
-Should start INH within ___ days of count recovery for 
previous +PPD
-Amlodipine increased
-Careful monitoring of sugars and insulin is needed - pt to 
contact his endocrinologist and record sugars
-Should complete course of Cipro/Flagyl for diverticulitis

radiology_notes.text:
ULTRASOUND AND FLUOROSCOPY-GUIDED TEMPORARY CENTRAL VENOUS CATHETER PLACEMENT

OPERATORS:  ___, M.D. (fellow) and ___, M.D.
(attending physician).

INDICATION:  ___ man with multiple myeloma, central line for
chemotherapy.

CONTRAST:  None.

SEDATION:  None.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  Consent was obtained from the patient after
explaining the benefits, risks and alternatives.  Patient was placed supine on
the imaging table in the interventional suite.  Timeout was performed as per
___ protocol.

Under aseptic conditions, sonographic guidance, and after infiltrating the
skin and subcutaneous tissues with 1% lidocaine, a micropuncture needle was
placed in the patent right internal jugular vein, just above the level of
clavicle.  Sonographic images were printed prior to and following needle
placement.  A 0.018 wire was advanced through the needle and into the SVC. 
Needle was exchanged for a 4.5 ___ microsheath.  Inner cannula and wire
were removed to place a 0.035 short ___ wire, which was advanced into the
IVC.  After appropriate measurements and removal of the microsheath, tract was
dilated with a 7 ___ dilator under fluoroscopy.  A 7 ___ triple lumen
venous catheter was then placed over the wire.  Catheter tip was confirmed
under fluoroscopy to be in the lower SVC.  Wire was removed.  Ports were
aspirated and flushed.  Catheter was secured with 0 silk sutures.  Site was
appropriately dressed.  Patient tolerated the procedure well and no immediate
post-procedure complication was seen.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated ultrasound and fluoroscopy-guided placement of a 7
___ 16 cm triple-lumen central venous catheter via the patent right
internal jugular vein and with its tip in the lower SVC.  It is ready for use.

CT OF THE ABDOMEN AND PELVIS WITHOUT IV CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ man, 2 days post-stem cell transplant for multiple
myeloma, now with new diarrhea and 7 of 10 left lower quadrant tenderness and
abdominal hernia on exam, evaluate for possible infection source of diarrhea,
pain.

CT OF THE ABDOMEN AND PELVIS WITHOUT IV CONTRAST

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector scanning is performed from the diaphragm through the
symphysis without intravenous contrast.

Comparison is made to prior examination of ___.

CT OF THE ABDOMEN WITHOUT IV CONTRAST:  The lung bases are clear.  The liver
is without focal lesions.  The gallbladder is contracted.  The spleen is
normal in size.  The pancreas is unremarkable.  A contour abnormality along
the right kidney was present in ___ and enhance normally, consistent with an
area of normal parenchyma.  There is a 4-mm non-obstructing stone in the right
kidney in the lower pole.  There is no retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.  There
is no hydronephrosis.  No focal fluid collection is identified.  There is some
mild fat stranding around the colon along the splenic flexure and some minimal
wall thickening in this region.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITHOUT IV CONTRAST:  The patient is status post
prostatectomy.  The bladder is unremarkable.  There is no free fluid in the
pelvis.  No pelvic lymphadenopathy is identified.  There is no pelvic fluid
collection multiple diverticula along the sigmoid colon.

On bone windows, there are degenerative changes involving the lumbar spine. 
No concerning osteolytic or osteosclerotic lesions are noted.  There is
unusual dystrophic calcification along the superior pubic ramus of the
symphysis.  This is stable compared to ___.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Acute mild, uncomplicated diverticulitis at the splenic flexure.

2.  4-mm non-obstructing stone in the lower pole of the right kidney.

INDICATION:  Neutropenia with known diverticulitis, now with new pain. 
Interval evaluation.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained after
the administration of oral contrast only.

COMPARISON:  CT scan dated ___.

FINDINGS:  The included portions of the lung bases are clear.

Within the abdomen, a previously seen area of inflammation surrounding colonic

The bladder and distal ureters appear grossly unremarkable.  Multiple surgical

There are dystrophic calcifications superior to pubic symphysis bilaterally

IMPRESSION:

SINGLE FRONTAL VIEW OF THE CHEST

Right IJ catheter tip is in the mid-to-distal SVC.  Mild cardiomegaly is

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, part of your care team. You're here for your autologous stem cell transplant for multiple myeloma. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I’m doing okay. A bit nervous, but ready to get this done. Is everything set?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re all set. First, we’ll place a central line so we can give the chemotherapy and stem cells safely. It’ll be done with ultrasound and X-ray guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they had trouble placing it. Is that a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of that. The team is experienced and will use imaging to make sure it goes smoothly. If needed, we’ll have backup options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line was placed successfully in your right internal jugular vein. It’s in good position and ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any side effects to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor for infection or bleeding. Let us know if you have pain, swelling, or fever at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting the melphalan chemotherapy today. This prepares your body to receive the stem cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will this last?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a few days. Then we’ll infuse your stem cells. You may feel tired or nauseated, but we’ll manage symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is the big day — we’ll be transplanting your stem cells. You’ve tolerated the chemo well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How will I feel after the transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be more vulnerable to infections for a while as your counts drop. We’ll give Neupogen to help your white blood cells recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the acyclovir I’m on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s to prevent viral infections. You’ll stay on it for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood counts are dropping as expected. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been a bit dizzy. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be from low counts or dehydration. We’ll check your labs and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re developing some swelling in your legs. We think it’s from the IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. I used to take Lasix at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give IV Lasix to help. We’ll monitor your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed left lower abdominal pain and diarrhea. We’re concerned about infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s pretty painful. Could it be from the transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we need to rule out diverticulitis. We’re ordering a CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows mild diverticulitis at the splenic flexure. No abscess, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s inflammation in small pouches in your colon. We’ll start IV antibiotics — meropenem — until your counts recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not now. This is mild and not perforated. We’ll treat it with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff test came back negative, so it’s not that. We’re continuing meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned a loose tooth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been wiggly for two days. No pain or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We examined it — no signs of infection. It should settle. See your dentist after recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The repeat CT shows improvement in the diverticulitis. No abscess. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll switch you to oral antibiotics — cipro and flagyl — for two weeks once your counts allow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is starting to recover. That’s a sign your stem cells are engrafting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your hepatitis B viral load. It’s undetectable — good. You’ll stay on lamivudine to prevent reactivation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver enzymes? They were high before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re still elevated — AST and ALT are up. We think it’s partly from past alcohol use. You’ll need close follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a drink in weeks. I’m trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll support you. Your liver can heal with time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures and urine culture are negative — no infection. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been feeling stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to oral cipro and flagyl for the diverticulitis. Finish the full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any dietary changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Low fiber for now. We’ll guide you back to normal eating gradually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been a bit high. We’re increasing your amlodipine to 10 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been on that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your endocrinology team reviewed your diabetes. We’re reducing your glargine to 25 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sugars have been stable. We want to avoid lows. Keep using your sliding scale for Humalog and record your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping it. Nortriptyline will continue for your neuropathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting Bactrim tomorrow to prevent infections while your counts are still recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my kidney function?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine is 0.6 — excellent. We’ll monitor, but it’s safe to start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Pain-free, eating well, and walking. We’re planning discharge in two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the INH for TB?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start it about a week after your counts recover. We’ll monitor your liver closely because of your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll remove your central line today. It’s no longer needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a little pressure. We’ll numb the area. It’ll be quick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Line is out — no issues. Site looks clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day — you’re going home. You’ve done very well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. What do I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, worsening abdominal pain, or shortness of breath — call us. Finish your antibiotics and monitor your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oncology, endocrinology, and primary care — all scheduled. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the hard work. Take care, and we’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — my hernia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s reducible and not causing issues. Monitor it. See surgery if it becomes painful or doesn’t go back in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels good to be on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for an autologous stem cell transplant for IgA multiple myeloma. The transplant was performed successfully after placement of a central venous catheter. During the hospitalization, he developed mild diverticulitis on post-transplant day 3, which was treated with intravenous meropenem followed by oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole, with clinical and radiographic improvement. He experienced transient lower extremity edema managed with IV furosemide, and his liver enzymes rose, attributed partly to prior alcohol use. His diabetes was managed with reduced insulin glargine and sliding scale lispro, and gabapentin was discontinued for neuropathy. He completed prophylactic antiviral and PJP prophylaxis, and was discharged home in stable condition with plans to start INH for latent tuberculosis and close outpatient follow-up.
